doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Racial mixing on records and Goodman integrating the stage
summary: Black and white musicians seldom recorded together; Jelly Roll Morton, Condon, Waller, then Goodman, Wilson and Hampton broke the barrier.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When you were doing this research in your early years of listening, did you start in your mind to be able to categorize things? Like when you heard something did you think of it as New Orleans jazz or Chicago style, or was there a difference between black and white bands for instance that you could hear?

Well there was in the sense that in the earlier days of jazz, black musicians and white musicians tended not to play together in public. And that included phonograph records for quite a while, although as we all know from the memoirs of everybody from

Armstrong on down, after hours was a different situation. But the division even stayed on records for quite a long time, although it was broken in small ways like Jelly Roll Morton playing with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings on that record in 1922 I believe or ‘23. And that I think happened because Jelly Roll’s music was published by Melrose Brothers in Chicago, and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings also placed publications with Melrose and so it was a natural thing that Jelly Roll would participate in some of these performances of the copyrights on records. On records also there is some infiltration you might say took place like Eddie Condon playing with Louis Armstrong on the famous “Knocking The Jug” session and then on the same day they did “I Can’t Give You Anything But Love,” and there’s Condon playing banjo with an all-black orchestra. And this continued with things like Condon again playing with Fats Waller on the famous five piece band session of “Minor Drag” and what was the other side, I keep forgetting the title. In any case the labels got reversed which was so spectacularly goofed up on Victor’s part, so that “Minor Drag” is a very fast tune and the other side is—

But it doesn’t matter. And the great breakthrough came about in the middle 30s when Benny Goodman hired Teddy Wilson to play as a member of the first Goodman trio that started on records actually. But Goodman decided we’re going to do this in person. So what he did was to play a set and maybe twice an evening, they would do this at the end of the set there would be a brief break and out would come the trio with Teddy replacing Jess Stacy on piano and Gene Krupa returning to the drums, and they would play maybe three numbers. And when Benny saw that this was succeeding, and believe me it wasn’t easy because he was told by people who were in charge at the hotels where he began this, the first one I think was in Chicago, and at first they say, “You can’t do that.” And Benny said, “Well I’m going to, fire me if you want to. He added Lionel Hampton on vibraphone, and the Goodman quartet was formed. And it all began with records first and then Benny, who was a very determined person as we all know from the anecdotes, forced the integration on stage. And when this happened, the situation where Gene Krupa left shortly, I think it was February 1938, Benny immediately had Hampton play drums with the band, which caused a bit of a stir again. He got that established and from then on it kept happening more and more. Roy Eldridge played with Gene Krupa and before that I think he was with Artie Shaw for a while. Artie Shaw hired Billie Holiday to travel with the band. He had terrible problems but he stuck with it as long as he and she could. We have to remember that Billie had a hard time and she was happy to quit because it was just too damn tough.
